title: English Vocabulary 3 · Units 73–74
description: Curated abstract nouns, productive noun suffixes and compound adjectives, with original examples, pronunciation guidance and use notes.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. The vocabulary targets follow the source themes and relevant exercises; all explanations and example sentences are newly written. Original passages, exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Checked full teaching pages, tables, language notes, common mistakes, exercise prompts and relevant answer-key entries for Units 73–74. Selected core lexical families, collocations and useful exercise-only targets without reproducing original prose.
audit.pronunciation: Broad British IPA is used for words and short expressions where confidently transcribed; uncertain multiword pronunciations are left blank. A live dictionary or speech system was not used to verify every transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is in English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Compared teaching and exercise pages to the supplied PDF and answer key; manually reviewed spelling, semantics, register, collocations, examples and TTS target length; performed local JSON structure, ID, provenance and audio checks.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio; no live VocabLab UI import test, browser TTS or speech-recognition test was performed.

units.title: Unit 73 — Abstract nouns
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 73. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Distinguish abstract concepts from tangible objects and recognise the usual article patterns.
Form abstract nouns from verbs and adjectives using -ment, -ion, -ness and -ity.
Recognise -dom, -th, -hood and -ship noun families, including non-obvious spelling changes.
Use abstract nouns without a suffix and distinguish key exercise-derived synonyms and related forms.

sectionsChecked: D: Abstract nouns without a suffix; common-mistakes note

items.example: Happiness is an abstract noun because it names a feeling rather than a physical object.
items.note: Names an idea, experience or quality rather than a tangible object.
items.section: A · Abstract nouns and reference concepts

items.example: My supervisor gave me useful advice about the interview.
items.note: Uncountable in this sense: a piece of advice, not an advice.
items.section: A · Abstract nouns and reference concepts

items.example: Her intention was to finish the design before Friday.
items.note: The noun related to intend; often intention to do something.
items.section: A · Abstract nouns and reference concepts

items.example: The campaign called for justice for the victims.
items.note: An abstract noun; general justice normally has no definite article.
items.section: A · Abstract nouns and reference concepts

items.example: Finishing the prototype was a major achievement for the team.
items.note: Achieve becomes achievement; a result or success.

items.example: A small adjustment improved the accuracy of the sensor.
items.note: Adjust becomes adjustment; the noun can be countable.

items.example: To my amazement, the old device still worked perfectly.
items.note: Amaze becomes amazement; often to someone's amazement.

items.example: There was a disagreement over the proposed budget.
items.note: Disagree becomes disagreement; often disagreement about or over something.

items.example: We noticed a clear improvement in response time.
items.note: Improve becomes improvement; usually improvement in something.

items.example: The laboratory needs more investment in equipment.
items.note: Invest becomes investment; may be countable or uncountable.

items.example: Finding a suitable replacement for the old motor took weeks.
items.note: Replace becomes replacement; a replacement for someone or something.

items.example: She plans to travel widely after retirement.
items.note: Retire becomes retirement; can refer to the event or period.

items.example: He showed great affection for his grandparents.
items.note: An abstract noun; affection for or towards someone.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: The museum has a remarkable collection of photographs.
items.note: Collect becomes collection; can mean gathered objects or the act of gathering.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: A combination of training and experience helped her succeed.
items.note: Combine becomes combination; commonly a combination of things.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: Customer expectations have changed considerably.
items.note: Expect becomes expectation; often expectations of or about something.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: Repeated network failures caused considerable frustration.
items.note: Frustrate becomes frustration; an emotion or the cause of that emotion.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: The main limitation of this approach is its high cost.
items.note: Limit becomes limitation; often limitation of or on something.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: Small businesses struggled during the recession.
items.note: Related to recede; here a period of declining economic activity.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: The new process achieved a reduction in energy use.
items.note: Reduce becomes reduction; usually reduction in something.
items.section: B · Abstract nouns with -ion and variants

items.example: A moment of carelessness caused the data to be deleted.
items.note: Careless becomes carelessness; the quality of not taking enough care.

items.example: She gradually regained consciousness after the operation.
items.note: Conscious becomes consciousness; used for awareness and wakefulness.

items.example: Her eagerness to learn made a strong impression.
items.note: Eager becomes eagerness; often eagerness to do something.

items.example: The friendliness of the staff made us feel welcome.
items.note: Friendly becomes friendliness, not friendlyness.

items.example: I appreciated her kindness during a difficult week.
items.note: Kind becomes kindness; a quality or a kind act.

items.example: He admitted that laziness had delayed his preparations.
items.note: Lazy becomes laziness; change y to i before -ness.

items.example: Politeness is essential when dealing with customers.
items.note: Polite becomes politeness; a quality of behaving courteously.

items.example: One weakness of the plan is its dependence on external funding.
items.note: Weak becomes weakness; can mean lack of strength or a flaw.

items.example: Regular physical activity is important for good health.
items.note: Active becomes activity; may name an action or a general level of action.

items.example: The manager has the authority to approve the request.
items.note: Can mean official power or a person or body holding that power.

items.example: Creativity helped the team find a cheaper solution.
items.note: Creative becomes creativity; a quality rather than a physical object.

items.example: Curiosity led her to investigate the unexpected result.
items.note: Curious becomes curiosity, with a spelling change.

items.example: Their generosity funded scholarships for several students.
items.note: Generous becomes generosity; note the changed ending.

items.example: There was open hostility between the rival groups.
items.note: Hostile becomes hostility; the abstract noun ends in -ity.

items.example: The popularity of cycling has increased in the city.
items.note: Popular becomes popularity; often popularity of or among.

items.example: The instrument's sensitivity must be checked before use.
items.note: Sensitive becomes sensitivity; useful for emotions and measurement devices.

items.example: She took up painting to escape the boredom of her daily routine.
items.note: Bored becomes boredom; the state of having nothing interesting to do.

items.example: Freedom of expression is a fundamental principle.
items.note: Free becomes freedom; not usually preceded by the in general statements.

items.example: The ancient kingdom controlled much of the coast.
items.note: King becomes kingdom; may be concrete (a realm) or an abstract political concept.

items.example: The novel examines courage, sacrifice and martyrdom.
items.note: Martyr becomes martyrdom; suffering or death for a cause or belief.

items.example: She achieved stardom after her first major film.
items.note: Star becomes stardom; celebrity status.

items.example: Experience can bring wisdom, but it does not guarantee it.
items.note: Wise becomes wisdom; the spelling changes.

items.example: The breadth of the river surprised the visitors.
items.note: Broad becomes breadth; physical width or figurative range.

items.example: Scientists measured the depth of the lake.
items.note: Deep becomes depth; note the irregular spelling and pronunciation.

items.example: We discussed the length of the training course.
items.note: Long becomes length; can refer to space or time.

items.example: One strength of the proposal is its simplicity.
items.note: Strong becomes strength; irregular change of vowel.

items.example: The warmth of her welcome put everyone at ease.
items.note: Warm becomes warmth; physical heat or friendliness.

items.example: The width of the doorway is just under a metre.
items.note: Wide becomes width; note spelling and final consonant cluster.

items.example: Many people change careers during adulthood.
items.note: Adult plus -hood describes a stage of life.

items.example: The group encouraged a spirit of brotherhood.
items.note: Brother plus -hood; may mean solidarity or an organised group.

items.example: She spent most of her childhood in the countryside.
items.note: Child plus -hood describes the period of being a child.

items.example: The documentary explores the challenges of motherhood.
items.note: Mother plus -hood; can refer to the experience or state of being a mother.

items.example: The neighbourhood has changed a lot over the last decade.
items.note: Neighbour plus -hood; often refers to a physical local area.

items.example: The author writes about identity and womanhood.
items.note: Woman plus -hood; an abstract state or stage, depending on context.

items.example: He missed the companionship of his former colleagues.
items.note: Companion plus -ship; the experience of having someone with you.

items.example: They built a strong working relationship over several years.
items.note: Relation plus -ship; a personal or professional connection.

items.example: Her apprenticeship provided valuable practical training.
items.note: Apprentice plus -ship; formal learning while working.

items.example: The universities formed a partnership for the project.
items.note: Partner plus -ship; a shared undertaking or business relationship.

items.example: The contract clearly establishes ownership of the software.
items.note: Owner plus -ship; having legal possession or control.

items.example: Library membership is free for local residents.
items.note: Member plus -ship; the status of belonging to a group.

items.example: He struggled to control his anger during the argument.
items.note: No abstract-noun suffix; an intense feeling of displeasure.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: Her belief in the project remained strong.
items.note: Related to believe; the noun has no added suffix.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: After the storm, a strange calm settled over the village.
items.note: Noun and adjective with the same form.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: There is a good chance of rain tomorrow.
items.note: Common pattern: a chance of something or of doing something.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: He never lost faith in his colleagues.
items.note: Often faith in someone or something.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: Fear of failure stopped him from applying.
items.note: Can be countable in some senses, but often uncountable as an emotion.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: Her sense of humour helped everyone relax.
items.note: British spelling humour; American humor.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: The proposal began as a simple idea.
items.note: An abstract noun that is commonly countable.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: With a little luck, we will finish early.
items.note: Usually uncountable in the sense of good or bad fortune.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: Safety is a fundamental principle of good design.
items.note: A rule or basic belief; distinguish principle from principal.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: She was shaking with rage after hearing the accusation.
items.note: An intense form of anger; also an exercise answer for fury.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: Please explain the reason for the delay.
items.note: Common pattern: reason for something or for doing something.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: The instructions made no sense to the new employee.
items.note: A noun with several abstract meanings; notice make sense.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: The sudden loss of sight would require immediate attention.
items.note: Related to see; also the ability to see.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: The speed of the vehicle was recorded automatically.
items.note: No nominal suffix; common pattern speed of something.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: A sudden thought made her check the measurements again.
items.note: Noun related to think; also an idea or act of thinking.
items.section: D · Abstract nouns without a suffix

items.example: Personal happiness matters as much as professional success.
items.note: Happy becomes happiness, with y changing to i.
items.section: E · Exercise-derived word families and contrasts

items.example: The new transport link brought prosperity to the region.
items.note: Exercise synonym for wealth; prosperous becomes prosperity.
items.section: E · Exercise-derived word families and contrasts

items.example: The report drew attention to a serious injustice.
items.note: Negative in- plus justice; both nouns can be abstract.
items.section: E · Exercise-derived word families and contrasts

items.example: The power cut left the entire street in darkness.
items.note: Dark becomes darkness; a quality or absence of light.
items.section: E · Exercise-derived word families and contrasts

items.example: Imagination is essential in creative problem-solving.
items.note: Imagine becomes imagination; an abstract noun ending in -ation.
items.section: E · Exercise-derived word families and contrasts

items.example: Love can be difficult to describe in words.
items.note: General abstract love usually takes no definite article; specific love may take one.
items.section: A · Abstract nouns and article use

items.example: She resisted the temptation to check her phone.
items.note: Specific temptation normally takes the; the textbook contrasts it with general abstract nouns.
items.section: A · Abstract nouns and article use

items.example: Her imitation of the actor made everyone laugh.
items.note: Imitate becomes imitation; a noun used in the exercise quotations.
items.section: E · Exercise-derived word families and contrasts

units.title: Unit 74 — Compound adjectives
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 74. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise the form, meaning and common hyphenation patterns of compound adjectives.
Describe appearance and personality using natural adjective compounds, including register distinctions.
Use compounds with particles and fixed collocations for travel, work, money and everyday descriptions.
Construct useful new compounds and distinguish spelling variants introduced in the exercises.

sectionsChecked: A: Form, meaning and hyphen placement

items.example: A well-known writer visited the school.
items.note: A compound adjective combines two or more elements; hyphens are common before nouns.
items.section: A · Compound adjective form and interpretation

items.example: A well-dressed visitor entered the reception area.
items.note: Before a noun, use a hyphen; after a linking verb, well dressed is common.
items.section: A · Compound adjective form and interpretation

items.example: The meeting felt like a never-ending series of questions.
items.note: Adverb plus present participle; often hyphenated before a noun.
items.section: A · Compound adjective form and interpretation

items.example: She chose a sky-blue cover for her notebook.
items.note: Noun plus colour adjective; describes a specific shade.
items.section: A · Compound adjective form and interpretation

items.example: A curly-haired musician was sitting near the stage.
items.note: Curly plus haired; can also be long-haired or wavy-haired.

items.example: The suntanned hikers returned from the coast.
items.note: Describes skin darkened by exposure to sunlight.

items.example: A blue-eyed child waved from the bus.
items.note: Colour plus eyed describes eye colour.

items.example: The rosy-cheeked child had been playing outside.
items.note: An appearance adjective built from rosy and cheeked.

items.example: The portrait showed a thin-lipped elderly gentleman.
items.note: Describes lips, not a person's weight.

items.example: The broad-shouldered athlete carried the equipment easily.
items.note: Broad plus shouldered; a body-description compound.

items.example: The left-handed student preferred a different desk.
items.note: The opposite is right-handed.

items.example: A long-legged bird stood in the shallow water.
items.note: Long plus legged; an appearance characteristic.

items.example: He wore an open-necked shirt instead of a tie.
items.note: Usually describes a shirt worn with the neck open.

items.example: She arrived on a brand-new bicycle.
items.note: Stronger than new; emphasises completely new condition.

items.example: The protective suit was too tight-fitting for comfort.
items.note: Tight plus fitting; often used for clothes.

items.example: Open-toed shoes are unsuitable for this workshop.
items.note: Used of shoes or sandals that leave toes exposed.

items.example: His explanation sounded rather far-fetched.
items.note: An idea or story difficult to believe, not a physical distance.

items.example: The absent-minded professor left his keys in the laboratory.
items.note: Describes someone who often forgets or fails to notice things.

items.example: Her easy-going attitude made the team feel comfortable.
items.note: Describes a relaxed, undemanding personality.

items.example: He remained good-tempered despite the delays.
items.note: Cheerful or not easily annoyed; contrast with bad-tempered.

items.example: The warm-hearted neighbours helped the new family settle in.
items.note: Describes kindness and sympathy, not physical warmth.

items.example: The quick-witted speaker answered every question immediately.
items.note: Fast at thinking of clever responses.

items.example: He became big-headed after winning the award.
items.note: Informal and disapproving; excessively proud of oneself.

items.example: I avoid sharing private matters with two-faced colleagues.
items.note: Disapproving: friendly to someone while criticising them elsewhere.

items.example: His self-centred comments ignored everyone else's concerns.
items.note: British spelling centred; American centered.

items.example: They thought the new manager was stuck-up at first.
items.note: Informal and disapproving; acting superior to others.

items.example: The workers threatened an all-out strike.
items.note: Means complete or using all available resources; common with strike or effort.
items.section: D · Compounds with prepositions or particles

items.example: Traffic moves slowly through the built-up area.
items.note: Describes areas covered with many buildings.
items.section: D · Compounds with prepositions or particles

items.example: Her family is relatively well-off.
items.note: Means financially comfortable; contrast with hard-up.
items.section: D · Compounds with prepositions or particles

items.example: I was hard-up during my first year at university.
items.note: Informal: having little money, unlike well-off.
items.section: D · Compounds with prepositions or particles

items.example: My worn-out shoes need replacing.
items.note: Used of items damaged by long use; can also describe extreme tiredness.
items.section: D · Compounds with prepositions or particles

items.example: The council plans to renovate the run-down station.
items.note: Used of buildings or areas in poor condition; can describe an exhausted person.
items.section: D · Compounds with prepositions or particles

items.example: The hotel has several air-conditioned meeting rooms.
items.note: Common before rooms, vehicles and offices; built around air condition.

items.example: The vehicle had bullet-proof glass.
items.note: Often written bulletproof; means designed to stop bullets, not absolutely invulnerable.

items.example: She booked a business-class ticket for the conference.
items.note: Travel category; usually hyphenated before a noun.

items.example: The shop offered cut-price furniture in January.
items.note: British English for sold below the normal price.

items.pt: isento de impostos ou taxas alfandegárias
items.example: Passengers can buy duty-free goods at the airport.
items.note: Sold without certain taxes or duties.

items.example: The gallery sells handmade wooden furniture.
items.note: Also written hand-made; made by hand rather than mass production.

items.example: The retailer offered interest-free credit for six months.
items.note: The -free ending means without; often with credit or loan.

items.example: We made a last-minute change to the schedule.
items.note: Describes something done shortly before the deadline or event.

items.example: Long-distance trains usually have more comfortable seats.
items.note: Often modifies journey, travel or relationship.

items.example: They have a long-standing disagreement about the contract.
items.note: Has existed for a long time; not necessarily about physical standing.

items.example: Off-peak tickets are usually less expensive.
items.note: Refers to periods of lower demand, especially in transport.

items.pt: de meio período; de tempo parcial
items.example: She took a part-time job during the course.
items.note: Part-time contrasts with full-time; a job can also be described as part time.

items.example: The so-called expert could not answer the basic questions.
items.note: Often signals doubt about whether the label is deserved.

items.example: The café offers sugar-free drinks.
items.note: -Free means without; do not infer that a product is free of all carbohydrates.

items.example: Preparing the documents is a time-consuming process.
items.note: Means requiring a large amount of time, not necessarily difficult.

items.example: The organisation kept its top-secret plans locked away.
items.note: Stronger than confidential; used for highly restricted information.

items.example: A world-famous conductor performed at the festival.
items.note: Means known in many countries, not merely locally popular.

items.example: A long-haired guitarist joined the band.
items.note: Contrast with short-haired; change the first element of curly-haired.

items.example: A red-haired actor played the leading role.
items.note: A productive hair-colour compound.

items.example: The wavy-haired woman was waiting outside.
items.note: Wavy describes hair that forms gentle curves.

items.example: The report contains first-hand accounts of the accident.
items.note: Information or experience obtained directly.

items.example: He received first-class service throughout the trip.
items.note: A travel category or a high standard, depending on context.

items.example: The first-born child inherited the family home.
items.note: Refers to the child born before their siblings.

items.example: A brown-eyed puppy looked up at us.
items.note: Eye-colour adjective; compare blue-eyed and green-eyed.

items.example: The green-eyed actress appeared in the new film.
items.note: Can be literal; green-eyed can also suggest envy in some contexts.

items.example: Keep the equipment inside a waterproof case.
items.note: Normally written as one word without a hyphen.

items.example: The archive uses fireproof storage cabinets.
items.note: Resistant to fire; does not guarantee resistance to any imaginable fire.

items.example: We travelled in a second-class carriage.
items.note: Can denote a travel category or inferior treatment.

items.example: A broad-minded teacher welcomed different opinions.
items.note: Means accepting different views or ways of life.

items.example: A narrow-minded policy would exclude talented applicants.
items.note: The opposite of broad-minded.

items.example: We served home-made soup at the gathering.
items.note: More commonly written homemade; made at home rather than commercially.

items.example: The reservoir is a man-made lake.
items.note: Contrast with natural; human-made is a gender-neutral alternative.

items.example: He prefers loose-fitting clothes in hot weather.
items.note: Opposite of tight-fitting for clothing.

items.example: Most of the tools were designed for right-handed users.
items.note: The opposite of left-handed.
